title.en: Manawydan and the Mouse: the Enchantment of Dyved
title.zh: 瑪南南與老鼠：迪維德之魔咒

region.zh: 威爾斯彭布羅克郡納伯斯（阿伯斯王丘）

texts.period: Recorded in the Red Book of Hergest, c. 1382-1410; Lady Charlotte Guest translation 1849

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1849), 'Manawyddan the Son of Llyr', eBook #5160

summary.en: A peal of thunder and a mist swallow the people of Dyved, leaving only Manawydan, Pryderi, Rhiannon and Kicva in an empty land; the two men turn saddlers, shield-makers and shoemakers and are driven out by every guild; a white boar leads Pryderi into a fortress where a golden bowl traps him, Rhiannon is caught by the same bowl, and Manawydan catches one slow mouse among a host of thieves and will hang it until a bishop ransoms the whole country.
summary.zh: 一聲雷、一團霧吞沒迪維德全境之民，僅餘瑪南南、普里德里、萊安儂與基克瓦於空土之中；二男子改行製鞍、製盾、製鞋而屢為各業公會所逐；一頭白豬引普里德里入堡、為金碗所黏，萊安儂亦被同一之碗所黏；瑪南南自賊群中捕得一隻遲緩之鼠、欲絞之，直至主教贖回全境。

sensitivity.note: The mouse is Llwyd's pregnant wife; the enchantment of Dyved is the bill for Pwyll's Badger-in-the-Bag against Gwawl — the Mabinogi's branches pay each other's debts.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849: They began a feast at Narberth, and when they had ended the first meal they went forth to the Gorsedd of Narberth — 'and as they sat thus, behold, a peal of thunder, and with the violence of the thunderstorm, lo there came a fall of mist, so thick that not one of them could see the other. And after the mist it became light all around.' And when they looked toward the place where they were wont to see cattle and herds and dwellings, they saw nothing now, neither house nor beast, nor smoke, nor fire, nor man, nor dwelling; but the houses of the Court empty, and desert, and uninhabited. So they four feasted, and hunted, and took their pleasure. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Wearied at last, they went into Lloegyr and took up craft after craft — saddles and housings of blue enamel (Calch Llasar), then shields, then shoes with gilded clasps — and in every town prospered so that none bought from the town's craftsmen, and the craftsmen assembled and agreed to slay them, and Manawydan refused to fight: 'we shall have evil fame, and shall be put in prison.' At Dyved, sowing three crofts of wheat, Manawydan found the first two eaten to the bare straw overnight; he watched the third, 'and behold the mightiest host of mice in the world, which could neither be numbered nor measured,' each climbing a straw to cut one ear and carry it away. He caught one sluggish mouse in his glove and hung it on a fork on the Gorsedd. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: A scholar, then a priest, then a bishop with retinue offered ransom for the mouse — a pound, three pounds, seven, four-and-twenty, then all the horses in the plain — and Manawydan refused them all: 'I will that Rhiannon and Pryderi be free.' 'That thou shalt have also.' 'I will know who the mouse may be.' 'She is my wife.' 'I am Llwyd the son of Kilcoed, and I cast the charm over the seven Cantrevs of Dyved. And it was to avenge Gwawl the son of Clud... for the game of Badger in the Bag, that Pwyll Pen Annwvyn played upon him.' It was his household who came as mice the first two nights, and his wife and the ladies of the Court the third; and she was pregnant — 'and had she not been pregnant thou wouldst not have been able to overtake her.' Manawydan's terms granted, the charm was lifted and Dyved restored. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Lady Charlotte Guest, The Mabinogion, 1849 (public domain); underlying: Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi, Red Book of Hergest

narrative.en:
The third branch of the Mabinogi is a domestic epic of unemployment, craft and commerce under enchantment — the warrior-god of the sea adapting to a market economy.

When the seven men had buried Brân's head in the White Mount, Manawyddan gazed on London and sighed: 'there is none save myself without a resting-place this night' — the third disinherited prince, his brother's throne held by Caswallawn. Pryderi offered the remedy of friendship: Rhiannon his mother, and the seven cantrevs of Dyved with her. The marriage was made before the feast was over; and the four — Manawyddan, Rhiannon, Pryderi and Kicva — sat at Narberth and began the circuit of Dyved in hunting and pleasure, so close in friendship that they would not be parted by night nor by day.

Then the enchantment. After the first meal they went to the Gorsedd of Narberth: 'a peal of thunder, and with the violence of the thunderstorm, lo there came a fall of mist, so thick that not one of them could see the other. And after the mist it became light all around.' And where they were wont to see cattle, herds and dwellings, there was nothing — the houses of the Court empty, desert, uninhabited. All their companions were lost to them without knowing aught of what had befallen, save those four only. They feasted and hunted a year; then weariness came, and Manawydan did the thing no epic hero does: he took up a trade. In Hereford they made saddles and housings, gilded and blue-enamelled 'in the manner that he had seen it done by Llasar Llaesgywydd' — craft learned from the otherworld giant. The saddlers of Hereford conspired to slay them; they moved on. In another city, shields; the smiths conspired. Then shoes with gilded clasps — 'there is not courage enough among cordwainers either to fight with us or to molest us,' said Manawydan, reading each guild's nerves — until the cordwainers too conspired, and Manawydan said: we will not slay them; let us go home.

At Dyved he sowed three crofts of wheat, and no wheat in the world ever sprang up better — until the morning he came to reap the first and found nothing but bare straw, every ear cut and carried off. The second croft likewise. The third he watched at night, arms in hand: 'the mightiest host of mice in the world, which could neither be numbered nor measured,' each mouse climbing a straw, bending it, cutting one ear, carrying it away, no stalk without its mouse. He caught one, sluggish and slow, and put it in his glove to hang at dawn. Kicva protested that it was unseemly; on the Gorsedd Arberth he set up two forks and noosed the string. A scholar came and offered a pound of alms; a priest offered three; a bishop with his retinue offered seven, then four-and-twenty pounds, then all the horses in the plain and their loads. Manawydan, hanging a thief, would take no price — and asked instead: Rhiannon and Pryderi freed. Granted — 'not yet will I loose the mouse.' The charm lifted from the seven cantrevs. Granted — 'I will know who the mouse may be.' 'She is my wife.' And Llwyd son of Kilcoed confessed the whole economy of the spell: he had enchanted Dyved to avenge Gwawl son of Clud for the game of Badger in the Bag that Pwyll Pen Annwvyn played on him unadvisedly at Heveydd's court; his own household had come the first two nights as mice; and the third night his wife and the ladies of the Court begged to be transformed — 'and she is pregnant. And had she not been pregnant thou wouldst not have been able to overtake her.' The terms were paid, the land restored, and the second branch's debt was closed at last.
narrative.zh: 馬比諾吉第三支乃一則關於失業、手工藝與商業的魔咒下之家庭史詩——海之戰神在市場經濟中求適應。七人葬白蘭之頭於白丘後，瑪南南望倫敦而嘆：『今夜惟我一人無處安身』——第三位被剝奪之親王，其兄之王座為卡薩瓦恩所據。普里德里以友誼為藥方：其母萊安儂與迪維德七郡。宴未終而婚禮已成；四人——瑪南南、萊安儂、普里德里與基克瓦——坐於納伯斯、巡遊迪維德狩獵為樂，友誼之深至夜與晝不分離。繼而是魔咒。初餐之後他們登上納伯斯王丘：『雷聲一響、暴風雨之猛、霧降而下、濃至彼此不能相見。霧後四周轉明。』而往昔所見牛群居所之處，今無一物——宮室空虛荒蕪無人。同伴盡失、不知所蹤，惟餘四人。他們狩獵宴樂一年；倦意生，瑪南南做了史詩英雄不做之事：改行從商。於赫里福德製鞍與馬衣，藍琺瑯鍍金『如其所見拉薩爾之工藝』——自彼岸巨人學得之技。赫里福德鞍匠合謀殺之；他們遷城。另一城製盾；鐵匠合謀。再製金扣鞋——『鞋匠之勇不足以與我戰或擾我』——直至鞋匠亦合謀，瑪南南曰：不殺他們；回家。於迪維德種三畝麥田、麥之優冠絕世界——直至收穫之晨第一畝惟餘光稈、麥穗盡失。第二畝亦然。第三畝夜間持械守望：『世上最龐大、無法計數無法丈量之鼠群』，每鼠攀一株、壓彎而斷一穗、負之而去，無一株無鼠。他捕得一隻遲緩者、納於手套以備黎明絞之。基克瓦言其不雅；於王丘上他立起兩叉、套繩於鼠頸。一學者以一鎊施捨相贖；一神父以三鎊；一主教攜侍從以七鎊、二十四鎊、繼而以平原上所有馬匹與馱貨相贖。絞賊之瑪南南分文不取——而只求：釋放萊安儂與普里德里。應允——『我尚未放鼠。』七郡之咒解除。應允——『我要知道這鼠是誰。』『她是我妻。』基爾科德之子盧維德坦白咒法之全部經濟：為報復普維爾於希維德廷中不智所行『袋中獾』之戲於瓜爾而施咒於迪維德；首兩夜為鼠者乃其家臣；第三夜其妻與宮中婦女懇求變形——『她有孕在身。若非懷孕，你根本追不上她。』條款付清、土地復原，第二支之債至終償清。

functions: Commerce as epic: gods and heroes as immigrant craftsmen driven out by guild protectionism
Legal theatre of the ransom: escalation of price until the true currency (people freed) is named
Debt-continuity between branches: the enchantment as compound interest on the Badger in the Bag
Doctrine of the catchable thief: the pregnant mouse as the one being with something to lose

title.en: Lludd and Llefelys: the Three Plagues of Britain
title.zh: 盧德與勒弗利斯：不列顛三災

region.en: Dinas Emrys (Dinas Ffaraon), Snowdonia, Gwynedd, Wales
region.zh: 威爾斯格溫內斯斯諾登尼亞迪納斯·埃姆里斯（古名迪納斯·法拉翁）

texts.period: Recorded in the Red Book of Hergest, c. 1382-1410 (earlier in Welsh chronicle tradition); Lady Charlotte Guest translation 1849

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1849), 'The Story of Lludd and Llevelys', eBook #5160

summary.en: Three plagues fall on Britain: the Coranians who hear every whisper on the wind, a shriek on May-eve that empties hearths and wombs, and a mighty magician who steals a year's provisions in a night; Lludd sails in secret to his brother Llefelys king of France, and they talk through a brass horn washed clean of its demon with wine — the healing of each plague prescribed, down to the two dragons that must be drunk, sleeping, into a mead-cauldron and buried in Snowdon.
summary.zh: 三災臨不列顛：能於風中聞一切低語之科拉尼人、五月夜使爐火空虛母腹落空的尖嘯、與一夜竊取一年存糧之強大術士；盧德秘密航行至其弟——法蘭西王勒弗利斯——二人以銅角對話、以酒洗去角中之魔；每一災皆有藥方——至於須使其沉睡飲盡蜜酒、葬於斯諾登之雙龍。

sensitivity.note: The buried dragons of Dinas Emrys are the origin-tale behind the red and white dragons of the Welsh flag; the center-of-Britain pit is dug at Oxford in this tale.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849: After a space of time three plagues fell on the Island of Britain. The first was a race called the Coranians, whose knowledge was so great that 'there was no discourse upon the face of the Island, however low it might be spoken, but what, if the wind met it, it was known to them. And through this they could not be injured.' The second was a shriek which came on every May-eve over every hearth in the Island of Britain, which went through people's hearts, 'so that the men lost their hue and their strength, and the women their children, and the young men and the maidens lost their senses, and all the animals and trees and the earth and the waters, were left barren.' The third was that however much of provisions and food might be prepared in the king's courts — even a year's provision — none of it could ever be found except what was consumed in the first night. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Lludd went to Llefelys king of France, and each came to meet the other with a single ship; they talked through a long horn of brass — 'but whatsoever words they spoke through this horn, one to the other, neither of them could hear any other but harsh and hostile words' — for a demon thwarted them, and Llefelys washed the horn with wine and drove the demon out. The cures: insects bruised in water to destroy the Coranians alone; and for the second plague, 'it is a dragon. And another dragon of a foreign race is fighting with it' — measure the island, dig at its exact central point, set a cauldron of the best mead covered with satin, and the dragons will fall fighting in the form of pigs, drink the mead and sleep. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Lludd buried the sleeping dragons in a kistvaen in the securest place in Snowdon — 'Now after that this spot was called Dinas Emreis, but before that, Dinas Ffaraon. And thus the fierce outcry ceased in his dominions.' For the third plague he armed himself and watched the banquet with a vessel of cold water at his side, plunging in when sleep oppressed him; a vast man in heavy armour came with a hamper and filled it with all the provisions, and Lludd fought him — 'the glittering fire flew out from their arms' — and threw the plague to the earth; the magician sought mercy and became his faithful vassal, and Lludd freed the Island of Britain from the three plagues. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Lady Charlotte Guest, The Mabinogion, 1849 (public domain); underlying: Cyfranc Lludd a Llefelys (Red Book of Hergest; earlier, 13th c. White Book tradition)

narrative.en:
Lludd and Llefelys is Britain's plague-diagnosis tale: a kingdom audited by three supernatural afflictions, and a king who cures each one with a different technology — poison, geology and a wrestling match.

Beli the Great had three sons, and Lludd the eldest inherited the Island of Britain; he rebuilt the walls of London and made them so beloved that the city was called Caer Lludd. His brother Llefelys, wisest of the family, had gone to France and won its crown with a daughter-heir. Then three plagues fell on Britain such as no island had ever seen. First, the Coranians: a race of such knowledge that no discourse on the face of the island, however low it was spoken, escaped them if the wind met it — a people whose hearing made them invulnerable. Second, a shriek on every May-eve over every hearth, that went through people's hearts so that men lost their color and strength, women their unborn children, youths and maidens their senses, and animals, trees, earth and waters were left barren — a scream with the force of a season's failed harvest. Third, the great theft: however much was prepared for the king's courts, even a year's provision, none could be found beyond the first night.

Two of the plagues had no known cause; so Lludd took the cure-seeking voyage of the era — in secret and in silence, lest the Coranians overhear the errand — to his brother in France. They met each other with a single ship each, embraced with brotherly love, and then had to invent a communications protocol: knowing the wind carried words to the Coranians, Llefelys had a long horn of brass made, and through it they spoke — and heard only harsh and hostile words, for a demon sat in the horn thwarting them. Wine washed the demon out; the horn becomes the tale's little parable of distorted counsel — every channel has its parasite, and the cure is a strong rinse.

Then the three prescriptions. Against the Coranians: certain insects, bruised in water, sprinkled over both races assembled as if for a peace-conference — the water poisons the Coranians alone, and the whole tribe was destroyed without hurt to any Briton. Against the shriek: diagnosis first — it is a dragon, and a foreign dragon fighting with it, and their battle is the outcry. Measure the island, find its exact central point (Oxford, in this telling), dig a pit, set in it a cauldron of the best mead covered with a satin cloth, and watch: the dragons will fight first as terrible animals, then as dragons in the air, and at the last fall as two pigs upon the covering, sink with it to the bottom of the cauldron, drink the mead, and sleep. Lludd folded the covering around the sleeping dragons and buried them in a kistvaen in the securest place in Snowdon: the spot was Dinas Ffaraon, and after that Dinas Emreis — the hill that Welsh legend keeps as the prison of the red and white dragons, whose contest Merlin would read for Vortigern in a later age. Against the third plague: a night-watch in arms at the great banquet, with a cauldron of cold water at hand — for the thief is a mighty man of magic whose charms put everyone to sleep. Lludd plunged himself into the cold water as often as drowsiness pressed, and when the vast armored man came in with his hamper — a hamper that could hold a year's provisions, a wonder in itself — Lludd followed, fought him until the glittering fire flew from their arms, and threw the plague to the earth. The magician begged mercy and paid with a vassal's oath: never again, and atonement for all the losses. Thus Lludd freed the Island of Britain from the three plagues, and ruled in prosperous peace to the end of his life.
narrative.zh: 《盧德與勒弗利斯》乃不列顛之災病診斷之篇：一個被三種超自然疾患查帳的王國，與一位以三種不同技術——毒物、地質與摔跤——逐一治癒災害的國王。貝利大王有三子，長子盧德繼承不列顛島；他重建倫敦城牆、深得民心、城遂名凱爾·盧德。其弟勒弗利斯最富智慧，赴法蘭西以婚約取得其冠。其後三災臨島，前所未見。其一為科拉尼人：其知識之強，島上任何言語無論多低、若遇風即為其所知——其聽力使其不可傷害。其二為五月夜臨於每一爐火之上之尖嘯，穿透人心——男子失色失力、女子失其腹中之子、少年少女失其神智、動物樹木土地水泉皆不育——一聲具有整季歉收之力之慘叫。其三為巨竊：王廷備糧縱多至一年之儲，除首夜所耗外盡皆無蹤。三災中二者原因不明；盧德遂行那個時代的求藥之旅——秘密而靜默，以免科拉尼人竊聽使命——赴法蘭西其弟處。二人各以單船相迎、兄弟相擁，繼而須發明通訊協議：知風可傳語於科拉尼人，勒弗利斯製長銅角一枚，經角對話——卻只聞粗暴敵意之言，因一惡魔居於角中擾之。以酒洗之、惡魔被逐；銅角遂成此篇關於扭曲諫言的小寓言——每一通道皆有其寄生者，解法是一次徹底的沖洗。繼而三張藥方。治科拉尼人：某種昆蟲搗於水中、於兩族如和會般集會時遍灑——此水獨毒科拉尼人、全族滅亡而布利頓人無一受損。治尖嘯：先診斷——那是一條龍，與一條異族之龍相鬥、其鬥即嘯聲。丈量全島、尋其正中點（此篇定為牛津）、掘坑、置最佳蜜酒之釜於坑中、以緞布覆之、守望：二龍先以可怖之獸形相鬥、繼以龍形鬥於空中，最後以二豬之形落於緞布之上、連布沉入釜底、飲盡蜜酒而眠。盧德以緞布裹住睡龍、葬於斯諾登最堅固處之石櫃中：該地先名迪納斯·法拉翁、後名迪納斯·埃姆里斯——威爾斯傳說保留此丘為紅白二龍之獄、其鬥後世將由梅林為沃蒂根釋讀。治第三災：盛裝持械夜守大宴、手邊置冷水一釜——因竊者為強大術士、其咒使人皆眠。睡意每至，盧德便投入冷水；待巨大披甲之漢攜大籃入內——一籃可容一年之糧、其本身就是奇觀——盧德隨之、戰之至兵器間火星飛迸、將災擲於地上。術士求恕、以封臣之誓償還：永不復犯、並賠償一切損失。盧德遂解不列顛島於三災，終身安治。

functions: Diagnosis-then-cure structure: each plague named as an agent (eavesdropping race, dueling dragons, sleeper-thief)
Etiology of Dinas Emrys and the red-white dragon contest behind the Welsh dragon emblem
Doctrine of the parasite in the channel: the demon in the brass horn as parable of distorted counsel
Charter of the vigilant king: sovereignty maintained by cold-water discipline against enchanted sleep

summary.en: The emperor Maxen sleeps beneath the shields of his thirty-two vassal kings and dreams his way up a river, over the highest mountain in the world, across the sea to the fairest island, into a castle at the mouth of a river in Snowdonia — where a maiden on a chair of ruddy gold is too bright to look at; he wastes away for a week until his page tells him the people revile him, and the dream is hunted down province by province until Rome itself is conquered for a Welsh bride.
summary.zh: 馬克森大帝於三十二藩王之盾蔭下入睡，夢中溯河而上、越世上最高之山、渡海至至美之島、入斯諾登尼亞河口城堡——其中金椅少女之美令人不能直視；他一週形銷骨立，侍童言百姓正譏其君，遂按夢逐省追索，直至羅馬本身為一位威爾斯新娘而被征服。

sensitivity.note: The tale historicizes Magnus Maximus (Macsen Wledig, emperor 383-388) and founds the origin-claims of Welsh dynasties and of the men of Armorica (Brittany).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849: Maxen Wledig was emperor of Rome, comelier and wiser than any emperor before him, and he went to hunt in the valley of the river that flowed toward Rome with two-and-thirty crowned kings his vassals. Sleep came upon him in the heat, his attendants set up their shields on spear-shafts about him and a gold enamelled shield under his head; and he saw a dream: journeying up the river to its source, over the highest mountain in the world, through the fairest level regions, down mighty rivers to the mouth of the largest river ever seen — a great city, a vast castle with high towers of various colours, the largest fleet ever seen, and one ship gilded one plank and silvered the next, with a bridge of whale-bone from the ship to the land. Not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: He crossed to the fairest island in the world, traversed it from sea to sea to rugged land, saw another island facing it, and a castle at the mouth of a river — the fairest that man ever saw, its hall with a golden roof and walls of glittering gems, two auburn-haired youths playing chess, a hoary-headed man in an ivory chair carving chessmen, and a maiden in a chair of ruddy gold: 'Not more easy than to gaze upon the sun when brightest, was it to look upon her by reason of her beauty.' He threw his arms about her neck — and woke at the clashing of the shields and the neighing of the horses. For a week he could neither eat nor be with his household, till his page told him the people reviled him, and the wise men prescribed the hunt: seek the dream by the road it seemed to go. Not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Thirteen messengers wearing one sleeve of their caps in front followed the dream's route — up the river, over the mountain, down the great rivers, over the sea to the Island of Britain, to Snowdon, Arfon, and Aber Sain — and found the castle, the hall, the chess-playing youths, the carver, and the maiden exactly as in the dream. 'Empress of Rome, all hail!' — and she answered that if the emperor loved her, let him come to seek her himself. Maxen came with his army, conquered the island from Beli son of Manogan, saw that every place was as he had seen it in sleep, and married her — Helen, daughter of Eudav son of Caradawc. Her bride-price was the island for her father and three castles, earth from Rome beneath the highest; and she made the roads of Helen Luyddawc from castle to castle. When Rome made a new emperor, Maxen besieged the city a year until Helen's brothers came with a small host and took it in a day by ladders; and Kynan's host, cutting out the tongues of their captured women, gave the men of Armorica their name of Britons. Not verbatim.

narrative.en:
The Dream of Maxen Wledig is the founding dream of Welsh political mythology — the tale that makes the Roman Empire fall in love with a castle in Snowdonia, and a dream the size of geography.

Maxen Wledig was emperor of Rome, comelier and better and wiser than any emperor that had been before him. One day he went to hunt in the valley of the river that flowed toward Rome, with two-and-thirty crowned kings, his vassals — not for the delight of hunting, the tale notes, but to put himself on equal terms with those kings. The sun was high and the heat was great, and sleep came upon Maxen; his attendants stood their shields on the shafts of their spears about him, set a gold-enamelled shield under his head, and the emperor slept.

And the dream is told as a journey of natural scale. He went up the valley to the river's source, and over the highest mountain in the world, and through the fairest and most level regions man ever beheld on the other side; down large and mighty rivers to the sea, to the mouth of the largest river ever seen — a great city, a vast castle with many high towers of various colours, the largest fleet ever seen, and one ship among the fleet larger by far than all others, one plank gilded and the next silvered, with a bridge of the bone of a whale from ship to land. He crossed to the fairest island in the world and traversed it sea to sea to its rugged far shore; saw another island facing it across a plain as large as the sea; and at a river's mouth a castle, the fairest that man ever saw — a hall with a golden roof and walls of glittering gems, two auburn-haired youths playing chess on a silver board with golden pieces, a hoary-headed man in an ivory chair with golden eagles carving chessmen with a steel file — and a maiden in a chair of ruddy gold: 'Not more easy than to gaze upon the sun when brightest, was it to look upon her by reason of her beauty.' She arose and he threw his arms about her neck, and they sat in the chair of gold together — until the chafing of the dogs and the clashing of the shields and the neighing of the horses woke him.

Nor spirit nor existence was left him. For a week the emperor who owned the world could neither eat nor drink with his household, nor hear songs and tales, but slept as often as he could, to see in dreams the maiden he loved best. His page — a king of the Romans, though a page of the chamber — told him the people reviled him; and the wise men of Rome prescribed the cure as a research project: send messengers for three years to the three parts of the world to seek the dream. A year they wandered and learned nothing; then the king of the Romans spoke the tale's key sentence: 'Go forth to hunt by the way thou didst seem to go.' The dream, in other words, has a road.

Thirteen messengers, each wearing one sleeve of his cap in front as the badge of envoys, followed it: up the river, over the mountain that seemed to touch the sky, down the great rivers, over the sea to the Island of Britain, to Snowdon, to Arfon, to Aber Sain — and the castle stood with its portal open, the hall, the chess-playing youths, the carver, the maiden exactly as in the dream. 'Empress of Rome, all hail!' 'What mockery is this ye do to me?' — and then the condition every dreamer must meet: 'If the emperor love me, let him come here to seek me.' Maxen came with his army, conquered the island from Beli son of Manogan, saw that every field and ford was as he had seen it in sleep, and married Helen, daughter of Eudav. Her bride-price founded Welsh geography: the island for her father, three castles — the highest at Arfon with earth brought from Rome for the emperor's health, then Caerlleon and Caermarthen — and the roads of Helen Luyddawc running from castle to castle, made by the men of Britain for no one but her. When Rome made a new emperor and wrote a letter of one sentence — 'If thou comest, and if thou ever comest to Rome' — Maxen answered in kind, besieged the city for a year, and took it in a single day when Helen's brothers came with a small host and their ladders. And the tale ends with an etymology of a nation: Kynan's host, settled in Armorica, cut out the tongues of their captured women lest they corrupt their speech — 'and because of the silence of the women from their own speech, the men of Armorica are called Britons.' A dream, a marriage, an empire — and the demographic charter of Brittany, all in one sleep.
narrative.zh: 《馬克森大帝之夢》乃威爾斯政治神話之奠基之夢——此篇使羅馬帝國愛上斯諾登尼亞一座城堡，而夢境之大一如地理。馬克森·烏萊迪格乃羅馬皇帝，其俊美、賢明、智慧勝於先前任何皇帝。一日他赴河穀狩獵——該河流向羅馬——偕三十二位加冕藩王；狩獵非為其樂，故事註明，而是為與諸王處於同等。日高而熱，睡意臨於馬克森；侍衛以矛桿立盾環繞、以金琺瑯盾為枕，皇帝遂眠。夢被敘述為一段自然尺度之旅。他溯河穀至河源、越世上最高之山、經人類前所未見之至美平原；沿大川巨河而下至海、至所見最大河流之口——偉大之城、高塔各色之城堡、前所未見之最大艦隊、其中一艦遠大於眾艦、板木一金一銀、以鯨骨之橋連舟與岸。他渡至世上至美之島、自海至海行至其崎嶇之遠岸；見隔海平原如海之大之另一島；於河口見人類前所未見至美之城堡——金頂寶石牆之廳、兩名紅髮青年以銀板金子弈棋、白髮老者坐象牙椅以鋼銼雕棋子、以及金椅上之少女：『其美令人不能直視，較仰望正午烈日尤難。』她起身、他擁其頸、二人同坐金椅——直至犬吠盾擊馬嘶將他驚醒。精氣全失。擁有全世界之皇帝一週不能與家人同食共樂、不聞歌與故事，只能盡量睡眠、於夢中見其最愛之少女。其侍童——雖為侍童、實為羅馬人之王——告以百姓正譏其君；羅馬智者遂開出藥方：遣使三年、遍三洲尋夢。使者漫遊一年一無所知；羅馬人之王說出全篇關鍵之句：『循夢中似行之路前往狩獵。』換言之：夢有一條路。十三名使者——各以帽前之一袖為信節——循之而行：溯河、越似觸天之山、下大川、渡海至不列顛島、至斯諾登、至阿爾方、至阿伯·塞恩——城堡門戶洞開、廳堂、弈棋青年、雕工、少女與夢中毫無二致。『羅馬皇后，萬福！』『爾等如此戲弄於我何為？』——繼而是每位夢者必須應付之條件：『若皇帝愛我，令其親自前來尋我。』馬克森率軍而至、自馬諾根之子貝利手中征服其島、見每一田野渡口皆如夢中所見，遂娶埃達夫之女海倫。其聘禮奠定威爾斯地理：以島賜其父、三座城堡——最高者建於阿爾方、其下鋪自羅馬運來之土以利皇帝健康；繼而凱爾利昂與凱爾馬森——以及自城堡至城堡之海倫之路，不列顛男子除她之外不為任何人修此大路。當羅馬另立新帝、寄來僅一句之信——『若你來，若你居然敢來羅馬』——馬克森以同式回覆、圍城一年、直至海倫二兄率小股部隊與梯子一日之內取城。故事以一個民族之詞源結束：定居阿莫利卡之基南部隊、割去所俘婦女之舌以防其敗壞語言——『因婦女緘默於其本族之語，阿莫利卡之人遂被稱為布利頓人。』一夢、一婚、一帝國——及布列塔尼之人口憲章，皆在一睡之中。

functions: Founding charter of Welsh dynasty claims: descent from the emperor's marriage into the line of Eudav
Etiology of the roads of Helen Luyddawc and of Caernarfon's Roman earth
Dream as map: the empire conquered by following a dream's itinerary — geography as revelation
Etiology of the Britons of Armorica: the tongue-cut origin of Brittany's name and speech

title.en: The Hare, the Salmon and the Grain: Taliesin's Birth from Ceridwen
title.zh: 野兔、鮭魚與麥粒：塔利埃辛生於凱里德溫

region.zh: 威爾斯格溫內斯巴拉湖（萊恩·泰吉德）

summary.en: Ceridwen boils a cauldron of inspiration a year and a day for her ugly son; three drops leap onto the thumb of the boy Gwion Bach, who licks them and knows everything, flees through the shapes of hare, fish, bird and grain of wheat — and is swallowed as a grain by the black hen Ceridwen, reborn nine months later, set adrift in a leather bag, and drawn up in Gwyddno's weir by the luckless Elphin, who names him Taliesin, the radiant brow.
summary.zh: 凱里德溫為其醜子熬煮啟示之釜一年又一日；三滴神液躍上男孩格維恩·巴赫之拇指、舐之而知萬事；他化野兔、魚、鳥、麥粒而逃——被化為黑母雞的凱里德溫如麥粒般吞下，九月後重生、以皮袋漂於海、被厄運青年埃爾芬自格維德諾魚梁拉起、命名塔利埃辛——光輝之眉。

sensitivity.note: The Taliesin birth-tale is the Welsh charter of bardic initiation: inspiration gained by accident, sovereignty of speech won through a shapeshift chase and a second womb.

narrative.en:
The tale of Taliesin is the Welsh initiation myth of poetry itself: inspiration brewed, stolen by accident, chased through the whole ladder of being, and born again as a baby who can out-talk kings.

In times past there lived in Penllyn a man of gentle lineage named Tegid Voel, whose dwelling was in the midst of the lake Tegid; his wife was Ceridwen, and their children were Morvran, Creirwy — the fairest maiden in the world — and a brother, the most ill-favoured man in the world, Avagddu. Ceridwen thought he was not likely to be admitted among men of noble birth by reason of his ugliness, unless he had some exalted merits or knowledge; so she resolved, according to the arts of the books of the Fferyllt, to boil a cauldron of Inspiration and Science for her son, that his reception might be honorable because of his knowledge of the mysteries of the future state of the world. The cauldron might not cease to boil for a year and a day, until three blessed drops were obtained of the grace of Inspiration; Gwion Bach the son of Gwreang stirred it, and the blind Morda kindled the fire beneath it, while Ceridwen gathered every day, in planetary hours, all the charm-bearing herbs.

Then the accident that is the tale's whole engine. One day, toward the end of the year, as Ceridwen was culling plants and making incantations, three drops of the charmed liquor flew out of the cauldron and fell upon the finger of Gwion Bach; and by reason of their great heat he put his finger to his mouth, and the instant he tasted the drops he foresaw everything that was to come, and perceived that his chief care must be to guard against the wiles of Ceridwen, for vast was her skill. The cauldron burst in two, and all the liquor except the three drops was poisonous: the horses of Gwyddno Garanhir died of the stream it ran into, and the confluence was called the Poison of the Horses of Gwyddno from that time. Ceridwen struck the innocent blind Morda on the head till one of his eyes fell out on his cheek — 'Wrongfully hast thou disfigured me, for I am innocent' — and then ran for the thief.

The chase is the ladder of being, in six shapes. He became a hare and fled; she became a greyhound and turned him. He ran to a river and became a fish; she became an otter-bitch and chased him under water. He turned himself into a bird of the air; she, as a hawk, followed him and gave him no rest in the sky. And at the last, in fear of death, he espied a heap of winnowed wheat on the floor of a barn, dropped among the wheat and turned himself into one of the grains. Then she transformed herself into a high-crested black hen, went to the wheat, scratched it with her feet, found him out and swallowed him. The magical duel ends not in an escape but in a conception: the grain of wisdom swallowed, the goddess pregnant.

As the story says, she bore him nine months, and when she was delivered of him she could not find it in her heart to kill him, by reason of his beauty; so she wrapped him in a leathern bag and cast him into the sea to the mercy of God, on the twenty-ninth day of April. Now Gwyddno's weir on the strand between Dyvi and Aberystwyth was worth a hundred pounds every May-eve, and that year its drawing was granted to Elphin, the most hapless and needy of youths. Nothing in the weir — and the weir-ward taunted that Elphin had destroyed the weir's virtue — 'there may be therein the value of a hundred pounds,' said Elphin. On the pole of the weir hung a leathern bag; they took it up, and he who opened it saw the forehead of the boy and said: 'Behold a radiant brow!' 'Taliesin be he called,' said Elphin — radiant brow, the name that would outlive kingdoms. The infant made a Consolation to his weeping finder in verse — 'Although I am but little, I am highly gifted... weak and small as I am... there lies a virtue in my tongue' — and years later, at the court of Maelgwn Gwynedd, when Elphin was chained in prison for boasting of his wife and his bard, Taliesin played 'Blerwm, blerwm' with his finger on his lips until all four-and-twenty royal bards could do nothing else, and then sang the great autobiography of the initiated: 'Primary chief bard am I to Elphin, and my original country is the region of the summer stars... I have been three periods in the prison of Arianrod... I have obtained the muse from the cauldron of Caridwen... Then I was for nine months in the womb of the hag Caridwen; I was originally little Gwion, and at length I am Taliesin.' Elphin was freed; and the boy who had been a grain of wheat became the chief of bards.
narrative.zh: 塔利埃辛之篇乃威爾斯詩歌啟蒙之入門神話：啟示被熬煮、因意外被竊、沿存在之全階梯被追逐、而以一個能勝過國王言辭之嬰兒重生。往昔彭利林地區有一位名為泰吉德·沃埃爾之紳士、居於泰吉德湖心；其妻名凱里德溫；其子女為莫爾夫蘭、世上至美少女克雷爾維、與世上最醜之人阿瓦格杜。凱里德溫思其子因醜陋恐不得入貴族之列，除非具備超凡之知識；遂決意依費里爾特之書之術、為其子熬煮啟示與學問之釜，使其以未來世界奧秘之知識得受尊榮。此釜一年又一日不得停止沸騰，直至取得三滴啟示恩典之福滴；格萊昂之子格維恩·巴赫攪拌、盲者莫爾達生火，而凱里德溫每日依行星時辰採集一切帶咒之草。然後是推動全篇之意外。歲末將近之一日，正當凱里德溫採草誦咒之際，三滴神液自釜中躍出、落於格維恩·巴赫之指；因液極熱，他將手指放入口中——一嚐之下便預知一切將來之事，並明白頭等大事乃是防範凱里德溫之詭計，因其法力廣大。釜裂為二，除三滴外之液皆有劇毒：格維德諾之馬死於其所入之溪，該溪匯流處自此稱格維德諾之馬之毒。凱里德溫擊無辜之盲者莫爾達至一眼落於頰——『你冤枉毀我，我乃無辜』——繼而追趕竊者。追逐即存在之階梯，共六形。他化野兔而逃；她化靈緹而逐。他奔向河流化為魚；她化水獺追之入水。他化飛鳥；她化鷹逐之於天、不給其喘息。最後，於死亡恐懼中，他瞥見穀倉地上篩淨之麥堆、落入麥中化作一粒麥。她化高冠黑母雞、走向麥堆、以足扒之、尋出他並吞下。魔法決鬥不以逃脫而以受孕終結：智慧之粒被吞、女神懷孕。如故事所言，她懷他九月，產下之時因其俊美而不忍殺之；遂以皮袋裹之、投於海中託付上帝之仁慈、時為四月二十九日。格維德諾位於迪維與阿伯里斯特威斯間海灘之魚梁每年五月夜產值百鎊之漁獲；是年其經營被賜予最不幸、最貧窮之青年埃爾芬。魚梁空空——梁守望者譏其毀梁之德——『其中或有百鎊之值，』埃爾芬曰。魚梁之桿上懸一皮袋；他們取下、開袋者見男孩之額曰：『看，光輝之眉！』『塔利埃辛就叫他這個名字，』埃爾芬曰——光輝之眉，此名將比王國長存。嬰兒以詩安慰哭泣的拾得者——『我雖微小，卻極有天賦……我雖弱小……我的舌頭中藏有一種美德』——多年後在格溫內斯馬爾格恩宮廷，埃爾芬因誇口其妻與其樂師而入獄，塔利埃辛以手指抵唇奏『布勒姆、布勒姆』直至二十四位宮廷樂師無一能作他事，繼而唱出受啟蒙者之偉大自傳：『我是埃爾芬之首席樂師，我原本之鄉乃夏日星辰之域……我曾三次居阿麗安蘿德之獄……我自凱里德溫之釜取得繆斯……繼而我在老嫗凱里德溫腹中九月；我原是小小的格維恩，而最終我是塔利埃辛。』埃爾芬獲釋；曾為一粒麥的男孩成為樂師之首。
